statement: Worker bees kill most of their kings, especially inferior ones, to prevent a multiplicity of kings from splitting the hive, and destroy royal cells when no swarm is intended.
On each foraging trip a bee goes from flower to flower of one kind only and does not visit another kind until it has returned to the hive.
The largest number of children ever born to a woman at one birth is five, which has been observed several times.
Older bees do the work inside the hive and are rough and hairy from staying indoors, while young bees do the carrying outside and are comparatively smooth.
In most fishes the gills are covered by opercula, but selachians (cartilaginous fishes) have none, because their skeleton is cartilaginous.
The great majority of horned animals are cloven-hoofed, and no solid-hoofed animal with a pair of horns has ever been found.
The dolphin bears live young directly and has two breasts placed near its genitals rather than high up, with no visible teats but two slits from which milk flows.
In copulating insects the female pushes her sexual organ up into the body of the male, the reverse of what happens in other animals.
Every animal with a coat of hair (counting the spines of hedgehogs and porcupines as hair) bears live young.
The female elephant carries her young for two years and bears only one at a time.
In the sheat-fish the female leaves after spawning while the male guards the spawn and fry, driving off small fish, for forty or fifty days until the young can escape on their own.
Eels arise from the so-called 'earth's guts', worms that grow spontaneously in mud and humid ground where sun heat causes putrefaction.
In both the large and small cicadas it is the male that sings and the female is silent.
Rabies drives dogs mad and is fatal to them, and any animal bitten by a rabid dog catches it and dies, with the exception of man.
Hair continues to grow after death, though it does not begin growing then.
In men, sheep, goats and swine, males have more teeth than females.
Animals born of crosses between different kinds can all mate and produce young of both sexes, except mules, which alone are sterile.
Semen is not drawn from every part of the parent's body, contrary to those who explain inheritance that way.
When a man comes upon a partridge brood, the hen rolls in front of him pretending to be lame, drawing him away until the young have escaped, then returns and calls them back.
Most fish eggs that are laid are destroyed before hatching, and fish produce great numbers of eggs to make up for this loss.
All cephalopods have eight feet, which are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in the octopus.
The she-bear gives birth while in winter concealment and stays hidden until she brings the cubs out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice; bears eat nothing while hidden.
Scaly fishes are always oviparous, and cartilaginous fishes are all viviparous except the fishing-frog.
Eels are neither born from pairing nor oviparous: no eel has ever been found with milt or spawn, nor with passages for spawn or eggs.
In some cartilaginous fishes, once the nutriment of the egg is used up, the embryo completes its development by connection with the uterus, so the egg is not released from the uterus.
Humans go grey on the head as they age, but this is not visible in practically any other animal except, to some extent, the horse.
The nautilus (argonaut) rises to the surface and, when a breeze blows, uses a thin web between its arms as a sail and lets down some arms as rudder-oars.
The wasps called ichneumons, smaller than ordinary wasps, kill spiders, carry them to a hole in a wall, seal it with mud and lay their grubs inside, and from the grubs come new ichneumons.
The human trunk has eight ribs on each side.
A female partridge becomes impregnated if she gets to leeward of the male, and often merely by hearing his voice or by his breathing on her as he flies overhead.
In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney lies higher in the body than the left.
The 'kings' (leaders) of a hive generate both their own kind and the worker bees.
Swans are musical and sing chiefly at the approach of death, flying out to sea at that time.
Elephants, being both land and swamp animals, have a lengthened nostril which, when they traverse water, they lift above the surface and breathe through, like a diver's breathing instrument.
Relative to body size, man has the largest and the moistest brain of any animal.
Worker wasps do not survive into a second year but all die as winter comes on, while the larger mother-wasps survive the winter in holes underground.
The female octopus, after laying her eggs, broods over them and loses condition because she does not go out for food during the hatching period.
A bee that stings dies because it cannot withdraw its sting without tearing out its intestines; once it loses its sting it must die.
In all other animals it is the lower jaw that moves, but in the river crocodile it is the upper jaw.
Crabs, crawfish and lobsters slough their shells, becoming soft all over, and they do so not once for all but over and over again.
The mullet migrates up from the sea into marshes and rivers, while eels migrate down from marshes and rivers to the sea.
When the land-scorpion's brood has hatched, the young eject and kill the parent, as also happens with the spider.
Scaly animals such as the serpent, lizard, gecko and river crocodile go into hiding for four months in the depth of winter and eat nothing during that time.

As a general rule all testaceans (shelled molluscs and the like) arise by spontaneous generation in mud, and differ according to the material: oysters in slime, cockles on sandy bottoms, ascidians, barnacles and limpets in rock hollows.
All feathered and hair-coated animals are infested with lice, with the single exception of the ass, which has neither lice nor ticks.
In all animals the brain is bloodless, has no veins in it and is naturally cold to the touch.
No bird with crooked talons (a bird of prey) lives in flocks.

Many birds do not migrate to warmer countries but hide where they are in winter; swallows have often been found in holes without feathers, and the kite, stork, turtle-dove, lark and others go into hiding.
Fishes are mostly divided into males and females, but specimens of the erythrinus and the channa are never caught except full of eggs.
The cuckoo is not a transformed hawk: it lacks the hawk's crooked talons, resembles the pigeon in head and claws, and is preyed on by hawks, which never happens between birds of one kind.
The eyes of all children are bluish at birth and later change to their permanent colour, which is not seen in other animals.
Horned quadrupeds that lack a full set of teeth in both jaws have a stomach of four chambers, and these are the animals that chew the cud.
Children usually resemble their parents or ancestors, but resemblance can be passed on after several generations, appearing in a grandchild but not in the child.
The brain cannot be the cause of any sensation, being itself as without feeling as any of the excretions; the sensory centre is the region of the heart.
The arm that the male octopus inserts into the female's funnel serves only for attachment and is not an organ useful for generation, being outside the male's seminal passage.
Man lives longer than any animal for which there is credible evidence, except the elephant.
Pigeons pair with the same mate until one of the pair dies, though occasionally a female mates with a bird other than her mate.
No animal has both tusks and horns, and no animal with interlocking pointed (saw-like) teeth has either tusks or horns.
The halcyon (kingfisher) breeds at the time of the winter solstice, unlike nearly all other birds, which breed in spring and early summer.
Animals that do not move about, such as testaceans (shelled molluscs and the like) and animals that live clinging to something, have no sexes, any more than plants do.
The torpedo (electric ray) catches its prey by numbing it with a shock residing in its body, and can numb humans too.
No pestilential (epidemic) disease is known to attack fishes as such diseases attack man, horses and oxen, although individual fishes do appear to fall sick.

The fig-wasp develops in the fruit of the wild fig, then flies into the fruit of the cultivated fig through its opening and makes the fruit stay on the tree, which is why farmers hang wild figs on fig trees.
A full-grown cock castrated by cauterizing the rump loses the colour of its crest, stops crowing and loses sexual desire; if castrated young, it never develops these male traits.
When the crocodile gapes, a small bird, the trochilus, enters its mouth and cleans its teeth, feeding itself thereby, and the crocodile does not harm it.
The cuckoo builds no nest but lays its egg, usually one, in the nest of a smaller bird, after devouring that bird's eggs, and the host bird hatches and rears the young cuckoo.
In cartilaginous fishes the male, unlike the female, has two appendages hanging down near the vent, and this sex difference is found in all species of sharks and dogfish.
Crocodiles spend the night in the water because at night the water is warmer than the open air.
The bee makes wax from flowers but does not make honey; it merely gathers honey that is deposited out of the atmosphere as dew.
Men castrated in boyhood never grow the later hair and keep a high-pitched voice, and a eunuch never goes bald.
The parts of an embryo do not all exist from the start; some are visible in the embryo while others are not yet formed, so they come into being in succession.
In all animals that can move about, the sexes are separate, one individual male and another female of the same species, whereas in plants they are combined.
In the smooth shark the young develop with a navel-string attached to the womb, so that once the yolk is used up the embryo is sustained as in quadrupeds, with a chorion and membranes.
Of the sense organs fishes have only eyes; they have neither the organs of hearing and smell nor any passages for them.
Deformed parents produce deformed children (lame from lame, blind from blind), and children often inherit their parents' peculiarities, including marks such as pimples or scars.
In most insects that copulate, the female is larger than the male.
Long, pointed eggs produce females, while round eggs, or eggs more rounded at the narrow end, produce males.
In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and crayfish) and in crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and stronger; only in the lobster is it a matter of chance which claw is larger.
Gestation in the dog lasts sixty to sixty-three days and never less than sixty, or if less the litter does not survive.
The hyena does not have both male and female genitals; each animal has one, but both sexes have a mark under the tail resembling the female genitals.
Human semen is white in every population; it is not black in any human population.
All animals are at first head-upward in the womb but turn downward near term, and in the natural course birth in all animals is head first.
The dolphin, the whale and all other cetaceans (animals with a blow-hole instead of gills) are viviparous, carrying an embryo rather than eggs, as do humans and viviparous quadrupeds.
The octopus hunts by changing its colour to match the adjacent stones, and does so also when alarmed.
The lion's neck consists of a single bone instead of vertebrae.
Very few birds breed within their first year.
A pair of eagles needs an extensive area to maintain itself, so it expels its fledged young from the neighbourhood and does not allow other birds to settle nearby.
The heart appears in the developing egg as a speck of blood that beats and moves as though alive, and two blood vessels lead from it.
Cranes migrate from the steppes of Scythia to the marshlands south of Egypt where the Nile rises.
In a high wind bees carry a stone as ballast to steady their flight.
In the cartilaginous fishes (selachians) the female is larger than the male, and the same holds for most other fishes.
A man begins to produce seminal fluid at about fourteen years of age and becomes capable of generation at about twenty-one.
Unfertilised wind-eggs are not relics of a previous mating: they arise in hens and geese that have never been impregnated.
The young of mutilated parents are not always mutilated, just as young are not always like their parents.
All polydactylous (many-toed) quadrupeds, such as the dog, lion, wolf, fox and jackal, bear their young blind, and the eyelids do not separate until after birth.

The butterfly caterpillar feeds and voids excrement, but once it becomes a chrysalis it neither feeds nor voids excrement; the same holds for all insects that develop from a grub, such as bees and wasps.
The skull of a woman has one circular suture, while the skull of a man, as a general rule, has three sutures meeting at a point.
Large animals have few young and small animals have many.
The fishing-frog (angler) has long thin filaments with rounded tips in front of its eyes which it raises as bait while hidden in sand and mud, drawing small fish that touch them into its mouth.
No animal is internally viviparous unless it takes in and breathes out air.
In all animals with blood the heart is the first part to appear distinctly formed in the embryo, being the origin of the blood-vessels and of the other parts.
Man is the only animal that laughs, and therefore the only animal that is affected by tickling.
